meta.purpose: Initial hierarchical scaffold identifying every merchandising fixture and non-merchandising space in the store. Geometry fields are null and get filled in after a diagram/model export is parsed.
meta.coordinate_system: Lay out the entire store in one shared file, at true scale, with each object positioned at its actual intended location on the store floor plan (not loose/unpositioned shapes). Use a consistent ground-plane origin (e.g. front entrance corner) across every tool/export used for this layout, so outputs from different tools stay aligned.
meta.object_label_rule: Every drawn object must be tagged with its 'object_label' value below, using whatever identifier mechanism the graphical editor provides for that purpose — a SketchUp group/component name, a SmartDraw shape's visible text label, or the equivalent in another tool. That value is the ONLY link between a diagram/model and this JSON: extraction matches on it (case/whitespace-normalized), independent of which editor or export format produced the file. An object_label with no match in this file is flagged, never guessed.
meta.drawing_rule: Each object = one rectangular block/shape representing the item's overall footprint (and height, for 3D tools). Don't model individual shelves separately — vertical shelf bands (see 'shelf_bands') are computed later by evenly subdividing a fixture's height, unless you deliberately choose to draw them explicitly (see 'shelf_sub_object_naming').
meta.uniqueness_rule: Nested/grouped objects are fine as long as every object at every level has a unique object_label — duplicate labels (e.g. from copying a shape/component without renaming each copy) break the link. In SketchUp specifically, use Groups rather than Components to avoid shared-definition name collisions.
meta.layout_notes: Ch. 1.3: perimeter placement for produce/meat/deli/bakery/dairy (flagged via 'perimeter_department' below) with center-store grocery in the interior aisles. Ch. 1.4: produce near the entrance, dairy toward the back to pull shoppers through center aisles. Ch. 1.5: grid aisle layout is dominant for supermarkets. These are placement guidelines for where YOU position each object, not computed coordinates.
